text: 217. Bng. ulkɔ, olkɔ ‘a shooting star; firelight’ and ulkɛṇɔ ‘to flame or blaze up’ (cf. p. 218); Garh. ulkā ‘meteor’; Bhal. sānhëlu ‘evening star’ (Kaul [2006 i: 336]) which is a compound < OIA saṁdhá̄- ‘twilight’ (12908) plus OIA uḍu- ‘star’ (1694) (Pa., Pk.) (?); here also Jaun. uḍāv kuria ‘pole star’ (with -āv probably a vālā suffix, second word < a side-form of OIA *kuḍa-¹ ‘boy, son’ [3245]) — Paš. ulík ‘spark’ (Buddruss [1959b: 28]). According to CDIAL, there is one possible modern reflex in Si., which is amazing as the OIA word is documented only lately; note however, S. ulo ‘spark’, G. “uḥlᵃkũ̄ ‘a rain of fire’ (LSI [i, ii: 347]) and M. uḍu ‘a star’ but ulkā ‘a meteor’ (also Ko. and cf. Ko. ulop, ulpā ‘inflammation; passion; heat’ and ulpāi to scorch’ which may derive < OIA LIP ‘inflame, kindle, burn’) which, like the Bng. and perhaps Bhal. forms, is related with OIA ulká̄- ‘meteor’ (2362). Here to be noted are also Deshi Prakrit ukkalo ‘heat’ (Bhayani [1988: 62]) and Ora. ullkā ‘a burn’. Note that there are other remarkable West Pahāṛī and outer language words related to the night sky: Bhal. gu-rot ‘milky way’ (see p. 705), Jaun. viã̄ṇia ‘morning star’ (see p. 714), Jaun. kirkiṭi ‘the Pleiades’ (Z.) (OIA kŕ̥ttikā- [3427], tatsama?), Sirm. “dhanishta” ‘asterism’ (Negi [1969: 433]) cf. OIA dhiṣṇya- with meaning ‘star, asterism (looking like the fire on the side altars)’ given by the astronomer Varāhamihira; Mult. māhõ māhĩã ‘the Gemini’ (O’Brian) a redupli- cation < OIA mithuna- i.a. ‘the sign of the zodiac Gemini’; Ind. pālʌ́ṅg and Jaṭ. palaggh pīhṛā (with second word < OIA pīṭha- ‘stool, bench’ [8222]) both ‘Ursa Major’ (lit.: ‘bedstead [seat]’) < palyaṅka- ‘chair of state, litter; Thronsessel, Tragsessel, Sänfte’ (7964) also found in Mult. and Kgr. as palag pihṛā and khaṭṭ, Garh. khāṭ, Brah. kaṭṭāk ‘Great Bear’ (< OIA kháṭvā- ‘bedstead’ [3781]) ‘con- stellation of Great Bear’, Shahpur dialect of Jaṭ. mã̄jā ‘constellation of Great Bear’ (< OIA mañca- ‘bed’ [9715]) and Kal. šen tári ‘big dipper constellation’ (literally ‘bed star’ with first word < OIA śáyana- ‘bed’). The quoted words have taken this meaning ultimately from Akkadian ereqqu ‘wagon; Ursa major’ (cf. in Europe Charles wain, Wotanswagen, gran carro etc., see p. 584 on more names of stars and asterisms). Some of the words are more or less old tatsamas.

text: 455. Bng., Khaśdh., Baur. gũzɔ ‘moustache’, Deog. gũzɔ or gũja < OIA gocchā- ‘furrow of upper lip’ (4269) (Pk.) with modern parallels almost only in the northwest: Ash., Kt., Wg., Gaw., Sav., K., to which I add Ora. maitā goccō ‘moustache’, Rom.Arm. konč, könǵ, gūᵉnč ‘beard’ and probably New. gvāc- ‘moustache’. An ex. from Bng. which is a typical threatening expression used by female bards during a quarrel: tēri ḍāṛi ḍɔũ gũzɛ kullu your beard burn.PR.1.SG moustache.OBL singe.PR.1.SG ‘I burn your beard and singe your moustache’

text: 470. Bng. gōṛu n.m. ‘a ball or handful of wool ready for spinning’, Kann. gōṭoċ ‘bundle’ (and koṭō ‘stack’?) — Ind. gòṛ karʌ́ṽ ‘to gather and bind grass or grains into sheaves’, Bur. gaáḍo -muċ -̇t- ‘(after cutting the stalks) to tie (the ears)’, Sh. gaáṛo ‘ditto’, Kamd. gˈoṭ ‘haystack’. According to Berger, Bur. is borrowed < OIA *gaḍḍa- ‘bundle, sheaf’ (3982), but this is a multi-morphic lemma and several reflexes derive < *goṭ(ṭ)a- , cf. also Or. goṭei-poṭei ‘gathering’ (Tripathi [1962(?): 208]) with second element also in Ora. poṭom ‘bundle’ (borrowed < OIA *poṭṭa-¹ ‘bundle’ [8396]), and with dental Sant. gəd to collect, heap up, gather’; thus perhaps also Kh. katiʔb ‘to collect, gather’ if containing a suffix.

text: 647. Chin. ḍṛagdir-pi ‘lightning and thunder’ — Paš. drūũg, drūũ̄g- ‘to thunder’ (cf. also draṅg- ‘to sound’) (Morgenstierne), second syllable in Bro. luŋd̪rʌk ‘storm’ (built with luŋ ‘air’ – Ramaswami [1975: 63]) — Jaṭ. dhaṛūknā ‘to thunder’ — Rab. hikirim- dikirim ‘the sound of friction between two clouds during monsoon’ (Roy [2011: 99]) — here perhaps also Kt. “oodrun” (Biddulph) or udařé sta ‘thunder’ (Strand) — Sang. doldoˈrok and ḍŏ̄ɣḍoˈɣok ‘thunder’, same as Psht. ḍoloxḍolox — Kh. dhadhir ‘thunder’ and and Munda Rem. digdag ‘flash of lightning’ (wohl zwei verschiedene Wurzeln), Bon. digdag ‘flash of lightning’ — Ora. ḍhurururū, ḍhurḍhurrnā ‘thunder’. An ‘expressive’ lemma with many allomorphs, but perhaps mixed with deriva- tion < PIE dʰerə-gʰ- (IEW: 251) i.a. Lith. dárga ‘squelchy, bad weather’ and Russian padoroga ‘tempest’ and ‘snow squall’. But note also similar forms in Western Tani like dō-ryak ‘lightning’ with dō < mesoroot #3570 *doṅ ‘weather formative; rain’. Notes: (a) Bur. tiṅgtoṅg ‘thunder’ (Biddulph) resembles Munda Kh. ṭhaṅka and Sad. ṭhaṅkā ‘thunder’ and all seem to constitute a separate lemma. (b) Another probably separate lemma: Kal. ḍiḍayoṅg ‘thunder’, M. dhaḍadhaḍāṭa ‘any loud thundering or roaring sound’, Khm. ˈdahdaŋ ni ˈduhduŋ ‘great crashing noise (esp. of thunder)’, Kh. ḍheḍhrel, ḍhɛḍhrɛl ‘thunder’. (c) Again somewhat separate are Psht. dandūkār ‘the noise of fire or thunder’ and Dm. daṇḍoˈrok ‘thunder’. (d) The following paragraph has already been discussed above p. 230, but is left here unabridged for simpler comparison: Kho. bumburúṣ ‘thunder’ and, probably borrowed from Kho., Wkh. bumbəˈriš ‘thunder’ are synonym compounds with second component < OIA ghóṣa- ‘noise’ (4528) (cf. Si. gosa ‘roar of thunder’). The first component derives < PIE *bhrem- ±‘make a noise’ but it cannot derive < OIA bhramará-² ‘large black bee’ (9651) which is reflected in Kho. bˈumbur ‘hornet’. Cf. Mayrhofer’s skeptical remarks on here unrelated OIA BHRAM ‘to be fickle, flicker, blaze’ (EWA), characterized by him as ‘elementary sound imita- tions’, but which probably has a semantically related reflex in different dialects of Paš. as blämúr and lāmbəl-bṛak ‘lightning’. However, Mallory and Adams quote this form and, moreover, they suggest that *bhrem- tends to mean ‘roar’ in Germanic (and similar in Latin and Polish) but means ‘bee’ in Sanskrit. Yet, the lemma for ‘bee’ has been listed by Turner separately as bhramará-² ‘large black bee’ (9651) and Mayrhofer believes that the ‘bee’ word can be equated with BHRAM only in the sense of ‘to ramble in a fickle way; unstet umher- schweifen’. Thus we have here a situation where the evidence from NIA is quite clear whereas the evidence from OIA looks rather blurred. The meaning ‘thun- der’ is also found in Greek βρoντή and in Latin (as Greek borrowing) frontēsia ‘thunder and lightning sign; Donner- und Blitzzeichen’. The two Kho. words are thus clearly reflexes of an OIA Vedic and a non-Vedic (OIA?) lect even though a hornet is bigger than a bee. ͡

text: 879. Bng. pɔgār ‘terrace wall of stones; (small) heap of stones and earth’ (also Kv.), Garh. pagār ‘wall; stair-like buttress of a field’, and Dari. parkhāl ‘wall (fence)’ — M.coch. pagāru ‘wall’, Ko. pāgār ‘bulwark’, Brj.-Aw. pagārã ‘enclosure (round a field, or a building)’ — Ora. pagar, pagār ‘rampart’ — are all related with OIA prākāra- ‘wall, rampart’ (8914) which is, according to Turner, possibly a sanskritized borrowing from Munda (e.g. Sant. pagar ‘fence’ and Mu. pagār ‘an elevated ridge with a drain on one of its sides’). The borrowing into IA must have occurred early, as is shown by Pa. pākāra- and Pk. pāāra-, and it is unlikely that it was borrowed e.g. from the Santal into the Bangan area much later; thus, also this is a strong suggestion that deletion of medial single consonants did not happen comprehensively; not only in Baṅgāṇī and other languages but also in Santali the -g- is still there. Next entry is similar. Note: Pr. pīr ‘wall’ does not seem to be related and is better derived < OIA (lex. and Kullūka Bhaṭṭa’s commentary on Manu-smr̥ti) prācīra- ‘an enclosure, hedge, fence, wall’.

text: 954. Kt. “pshu2, pashi, pashu” ‘hill’ and “pashun” ‘spur of a hill’ (Davidson) and pāṣi ‘mountainside; slope’ (Strand); Mayrhofer quotes Kt. parši ‘mountain’ and Ash. and Wg. paṣú̄ ‘rock’ (the first word probably borrowed into Psht. pˈarxa ‘boulder, rock’) to which are to be added Bng. paśɔ1 n.m. ‘stone’, Deog. paśɔ pāṇɔ ‘(as a Brahmin) to presage’ (this is done with the help of an oracle book sã̄ċɔ [also sɔ̃ċɔ and poet. sɔ̃ċɔ̃dri, sɔ̃ċotri < OIA lex. sañca- ‘a copy-book’ and also found in M. sã̄cā ‘a mould’ and sañcikā ‘an album’] and throwing of an oblong dice, therefore the lit. meaning ‘to throw a dice’), S. pahṇī ‘gravel’, Ko. pākaṇ ‘granite’ and perhaps (another dialect?) pāz ‘a rock’, Garh. pakhāṇ ‘mountain, hill’ (Catak [1959: 41]) and pākhāṇū ‘mountain peaks’ (Catak [1973: 200]) or pākhāṇ, and pākhā ‘part/section of a mountain; slope’ (Bhatt 1975 [vikrama 2032]: 377 and elsewhere), Dari. pākhān ‘precipice’, and borrowed into Dravidian Kurkh. pəkhna ‘stone’. They correspond (phonologically) exactly with OIA pāṣí̄- ‘stone, rock’ (8140) and pāṣāṇá- ‘stone’ (8138) which are thus in turn clearly semantically connected with OIA *pāhāḍa- ‘rock, hill’ (8141); Mayrhofer (EWA) considers in addition connection with PIE *pel(e)s- ‘rock’ and Greek πέλλα ‘stone’. Note also Arm. pal ‘rock’ which Martirosyan (2008: 437), however, regards to be a Mediterranean and/or European substratum term, and note PN *pʰal-a ‘stone’ (CINCL 87). Martirosyan’s opinion is shared by Furnée (KEV: 162) and Beekes (PREG: 52).

text: 1194. Ku. burũ̄ṭhiyā ‘thumb’, N. buḍi ʌũla ‘thumb’ (Z.), Paš.deg. bōṇḍˈai aṅgoṛek ‘thumb’, PKT *buḍɦa and buḍɦi aṅgul ‘thumb’, Ora. buṛhī aṅglī and Sant. buḍhə kɔṭuʔp ‘thumb’ (kɔṭuʔp ‘finger’) with first components < OIA *buḍḍha- ‘old’ (9271) plus aṅgúli- ‘finger’ (135); here semantically closely related is also B.roh. buijjá oũl ‘thumb, big toe’ with first word related with OIA vardhyate ‘is caused to grow’ (11386a) (with modern reflexes in West Pahāṛī); N. jeṭhi aũli ‘thumb’ (Turner) with first component < OIA jyéṣṭha- ‘eldest’ (5286) — Kal. ǰeṣṭ ạ́ṅgu ‘thumb’, Paš. ǰiṣṭˈī aṅguṛˈēk ‘thumb’, Kt. “jasht angur” ‘thumb’ (Konow) (all three built like the N. Turner form, see also ATLAS 119 for various first components), Ash. ˈgăṇi-aˈṅur ‘thumb’, Pal. ghān aṅgúṛu ‘thumb’ and Woṭ. gen aṅgíṛ ‘thumb’ with first components meaning ‘elder’; probably also Psht. ɣaṭa-gūta ‘thumb’ with first component meaning ‘great in rank’. This is a case of intra Indo-Aryan ‘calques’ (p. 222) extending into Iranian; however, there are quite strong arguments to show that ‘thumb’ as ‘old finger’ has originally come from Munda or ‘North Indian’ (see p. 959).

text: 1671. Kann. hurang (hu-rang) ‘a large wooden bolt used to fasten up a door’, Him. hūṛ ‘a bolt above a door’, Ku. huv, hu, huḷ ‘wooden bar or bolt’, Kṭg. and Kc. hʊ̀ṛnõ ‘to bolt (a door)’, Him. huṛnu ‘to shut in’ and húṛ ‘bolt above a door’ — Bi. hurkā ‘bolt of lock’, B. huḍkā ‘a latch, bolt’ — B. huṛᵃkā ‘bolt’, Ora. huṛuk ‘wooden bolt for fastening door’, Mu. huṛkā ‘wooden bar for a door’, Sant. hurkəṛ ‘wooden bar or bolt (of a door)’ — Ind. hú̄l ‘a post pressed from inside against the front door at night as a safety measure’, Kt. vúḍ ‘bolt (of door or window)’, Sh.gil. ŭˈdȋ ‘bolt’, Sh.koh. udí ‘bar of door’ — Psht. hūl ‘a bar or bolt for a door, a prop to a matted shutter’ < OIA *huḍa- - and OIA lex. huḍakka- ‘bolt or bar’ (14135a). text: 22. (a) Bng. kuti ‘tickling’ and kutiāṇɔ ‘to tickle’, Jaun. (Z.) kustiyāvṇɔ, Rp. kutkutyai ‘tickling’, N. kutkuti ‘ticklishness’, Rab. kut-kutā- ‘to tickle’, Chit. kitikiti, Deog. kutlaɔṇɔ ‘to tickle s.o.’, Ku. kutkyāi — Bur. qíqit -̇t- and Bur.ys. qétu-qétu both ‘to tickle’, Kho. qéti-qéti, K. kᵃta-kᵃta ‘tickling’, Kamd. katˈakatak ku ‘tickle’, Kal. kitikíti kárik or tikitíki kárik ‘to tickle’ (with karék ‘to tickle someone’), Pr. kiṭə-kiṭək li- ‘to tickle’ and kitəkˈitək ‘tickling’. — B. and Or. kutukutu ‘tickling’, B.roh. kútu ‘feeling funny when touching some parts of the body’ — L. kutkutāṛī, Jaṭ. kutkutāṛī ‘tickling’, S. kutikuti ‘tickling’ and S. kitikitāiṇu ‘to tickle’. (b) Bng. khitkhitāṇɔ ‘to tickle’ — Ind. khít-khitʰ karʌ́v ‘to tickle s.o.’, xìt-xitʰ karʌ́v ‘to tickle (the sole of the foot)’, xʌtì ‘tickling’, xutkulĩ̄ ‘tickle’ (where -kulĩ̄ is related with Pers. kilkil ‘tickling’; also in M.wār. kiċkuli ‘tickling’). (c) Bng. gidgidi ‘tickling’, Khaśdh. gutiauṇɔ ‘to tickle s.o.’ There are also P. gutgutāuṇa ‘to tickle’, M. gudgudī ‘titillation’, Ko.kuṇ. gudguli ‘tickling’, H. gudgudānā ‘to tickle’, B.roh. gudguti ‘backbiting person’, Brah. ɣutlū ‘tickling’ and Deshi Prakrit gilagilāviaṁ (G. galgaliyāṁ) and second member in the near-synonym compound gañjolliaṁ (with first member < OIA *gañj- ‘press, ram’ [3960]) all ‘tickling’ (Bhayani [1988: 71]) — Ora. gutgutū, gutgutī ‘tickling’. I may point out that the PIE root for the very obviously onomatopoeic ‘tickle’ is *geid-, described by Mallory and Adams (2007: 377) as a “Germanic-Armenian isogloss”; however, Watkins suggests the alternative forms of this “expressive root” tit-, tik-, kit- and Lipp quotes Old Nordic kitla and German kitzeln (2009 i: 59), see also Kroonen on Proto-Germanic *kit(t)ōn- ‘to tickle’ (2013: 289). Moreover, many forms compare also with Munda and Mon- Khmer forms, e.g. Bon. kitiʔk- ‘to tickle’, PMK *[k]ti[ ]k ‘to tickle’, Khasi ktik ‘to tickle’, and in case of Deshi Prakrit gilagilāviaṁ and G. galgaliyāṁ one may even think of influence of PIE *gelēi- ‘smile, laugh’, all of which suggests contamination of onomatopoeic forms of different language families.

text: 54. Bng. gād ‘a deep stream or (small) river (which is difficult to cross)’, gādɔ and gɔdrɔ ‘deep (e.g., a hole)’ and gɔdrɔ ‘below, lower’ (with -rɔ1 suffix) (e.g. in gɔdri bāṭ ‘the path below [the one where I am])’, Ku. and Garh. gadhera, gadheri, gadhyār ‘a small brook in the hills’, Rp. gədərɔ ‘brook’, Garh. gadnī, gadan, gadnā, gadrā, gaderā ‘brook, rivulet’ — Kurkh. gədi ‘river; a pit or a deep place’ — Kal. bisgúdyak (bis- gúd-yak ‘back.of.head-indentation-DIM) ‘the indentation on the neck just below the base of the skull’, Gaw. gūd ‘lake, pool’, — Wg. güd ‘a deep place (tiefe Stelle)’ as in yi ˈāva-kan güd oy ‘in this water is a deep place, i.e. one cannot wade through’,  (-ü- comes from older -a-; cf. here also Av. guða- ‘depth’), Paš.deg. godˈar ‘place by the river that women go to collect water’. The words are certainly not derived from OIA *gadda-¹ ‘sediment, mud’ which is found in Bng. as gɔdɔ1 ‘dirt’ (cf. also M. gadaḷ ‘dirtiness’ and Jaṭ. gadhal ‘dirt, mud [in water]’), even though Ku. gād ‘muddy running water’ appears to have been influenced by the lemma and Paliwal accordingly suggests for the above Ku. forms derivation < *gadda-dhārā-. This opposes the Bng. and Wg. forms which can be compared on the one side with PIE *gȗādʰ- ‘dive’ and derived Av. vi-gāθa- ‘ravine’, but on the other side note also Western Himalayish Baram gudul ‘river’. Regarding semantics cf. sub OIA gādhá- ‘ford; shallow’ (4127), Sh. ga ‘small mountain stream’ and Sh.koh. ga sg., gahí pl. ‘mountain stream’; to these is to be added P. gāhaṇ ‘a ford, fording’. The above words actually correspond semantically with OIA agādha- ‘deep’ which might have a reflex in ugad-xwaṛ ‘name of a river in the Swat Valley’ (second word Psht.) (De Chiara [2020: 230]), and which may have a morphological but not semantical reflex in Jaṭ. hāth ‘shallow; depth of water up to chin’ (with word-final devoicing) and vice versa Shahpur dialect of Jaṭ. hāhū ‘very deep’. But cf. also OIA (Tāṇḍyabr.) ugragādha- ‘any unfathomable or dangerous depth (of a river &c )’. FLII 20.1.35 suggests possible derivation of gādhá- < PIE *gȗeh2dʰ- ‘to plunge, immerse; eintauchen’ which matches quite well with the quoted modern meanings. For different etymological suggestions see also Ollett (2014b: 159). As a last remark on this difficult lemma I want to add that there are also Munda Kor. gada ‘river’, in all likelihood etymologically connected with Sant. etc. gaɖa ‘river’ (cf. OIA *gaḍḍa- ‘hole, pit’ [3981]), and Kol gadlu ‘deep’, Koda gadʰa ‘deep’ and Sant. (Rashidpur) gata ‘deep’. One wonders whether here a PIE root and a Munda or rather ‘North India’ lemma got blended.

text: 115. ‘Butterfly’ and ‘flying-fluttering’ (a) Deog. phiphṛi and phimphṛi ‘butterfly’, Kṭg. phímpəṛi ‘butterfly’ (wrongly put in the Addenda and Corrigenda sub pipīlá- ‘ant’ [8201]), Khaśdh. putuṛi ‘butterfly’, Ku. purputaī ‘butterfly’, Jaun. pōtōṭhō, Him. phĩphṛī, Khāśi. phāphṛi, Pāḍ. pāpṛi, Bhal. papṛi, pepri, Khaś. phāphṛi, Bhad. pāpṛi or pepṛõ all ‘butterfly’ — Kurkh. pəpəla ‘butterfly’ — Paṭṭ. phərphitig ‘butterfly’, Chin. pharphiṭig (or phārpitig, Kaul [2006 ii: 42]) ‘butterfly’, Gar. phremolig ‘butterfly’, K. pam pũ̄par ‘butterfly’ (Sachdeva et al. [2010: 60]) — Ind. phirphirì̄ ‘butterfly’, Bur. asqúriṅe phirán ‘butterfly’, Tor.cail. pʌrparʌk ‘moth’, Paš. pheṭiyák ‘butterfly’ — Psht. parkai ‘butterfly’ — Khet. phōpuṭ ‘butterfly’, S. popṭu ‘butterfly’, Jaṭ. popaṭ ‘butterfly, moth’ and bhabbaṭ ‘moth’, Ko.S. phulpã̄khrũ ‘butterfly’ (with second component < OIA pakṣín- ‘bird’), Ko.kaṇ. birbirẽ ‘butterfly’ — Sad. paplā ‘butterfly’ and Kh. pampla, phamphlaʔ which seems (like first word in K. pam pũ̄par) to have Austro-Asiatic parallels: Bahnaric Cua pʌm pil ‘moth, butterfly’, Proto-Vietic *paːmə ‘butterfly’, Sant. pipṛiaṅ ‘butterfly’ and Bon. laʔlaʔp ‘butterfly’, and Mon-Khmer LwAd. poopil ‘butterfly’. Perhaps also related are Kho. pulmuṇḍuk ‘butterfly’, Sh.gur. phōpal ‘butterfly’, Wkh. pilek-miˈlek or pilpilak ‘butterfly’ and Ishk. parparanuk ‘butterfly’, Kamd. prüšpˈulik ‘butterfly; moth’, Bal. pirrik ‘butterfly’. Cf. PIE *pelpel- ‘butterfly’, Latin pāpiliō, Arm. xipilik (loanword?), all ‘butterfly’; cf. also Common Kartvelian *perpel-‘butterfly; wing’, Zan (Laz dialect) parpal-i, Megrelian parpal-ia//parpal-i ‘butterfly; twisting/swirling’; cf. also PTB *pur ‘butterfly’ which, however, is not found in Tib., the only geographically plausible near form is Kann. pʰərpʰitig ‘butterfly’. Generally one can say that many of the above forms got not only ‘indianized’ i.e. they are examples for linguistic naturalization (on this term see p. 223), but also intersected with similar-sounding words e.g. from Austro-Asiatic and Dravidian, and last but not least some of the words may have also been influenced by reflexes of OIA pattrá- ‘wing’ with -ṭṭ- extension (7733) and by the following lemma (b). Cf. also Proto-Dravidian *papla ‘butterfly’ (Pfeiffer [1972: 20f.]) and e.g. Ora. paplā ‘butterfly’, and simimlar “sound-symbolism” forms in Munda (Kuiper [1962: 82]). (b) Bng., Deog. and West Pahāṛī far ‘the sound of a bird’s flight’, Khaśdh. phʌr-phʌr ‘ditto’, Garh. phurr ‘sound of a flying bird’ and pharṛī ‘a banner’, N. pharpharāhaṭ, phyār-phyār, pher-pher all ‘fluttering’ and Khm. phur phur ‘high in the air’, Rab. furut ‘sound of flying away a bird’ (Roy [2011: 100]) — Jaḍ. phur-phurja ‘to fly’ (Z.), Pur. phurcas ‘to fly’ (with infinitive/verbal noun ending), Balt., Nyam-kad and Tib. phur ‘(to) fly’ (other Tibetan forms are phir-, bur-, ur-), New. pharphar, phyār phyār ‘fluttering’ — Brah. firfir and paṛpaṛ ‘flutter; fluttering’ — Ind. phʌ́r ho- ‘to fly’, also in some Sh. dialects puř- and phuri- ‘fly’, Kho. pár ‘sound of bird’s wings flapping’, Bur.ys. pər ɛt- ‘to fly’ — Rj.jaip. bharbhar ‘the noise made by the flying of a bird’ — H. phurr ‘whirring sound (of wings)’ — Sant. phur phur ‘making buzzing, whirring sounds’ (one of Bodding’s examples is with a quail). There is certainly an onomatopoeic component in this lemma and it is unclear to which extend the Tibetan verb was borrowed into surrounding languages. Note also Pers. parper ‘fluttering’, and there are more similar Munda forms: reflexes of Proto-Kherwarian apir ‘to fly’ are found in several modern Munda languages and in Nih. aphir ‘to fly’ (Pinnow [K 501]). Whether or not there is IE influence in this lemma is difficult to say. Influence of OIA *spharati¹ ‘throbs, quivers’ (13820) and of sphuráti¹ ‘spurns, darts’ (13849)  can be excluded because of the different semantic reflexes in Bng. phɔrphɔrāṇɔ ‘to whirl or swirl up (as wind)’ and phurṇɔ ‘to twitch, bat (eye[lash], muscle)’. But it is clear that it is another example of what Mallory and Adams (already quoted above p. 778) describe as an instance “where onomatopoeia has supported their survival.” Cf. also PN *pʰar- ‘to flutter, fly’ (CINCL 101), PAA *par ‘to fly’ (also reflected in PMU **pER) and even Swab. pfurren ‘to flare up with whooshing, buzzing speed’ (von Schmid).

text: 149. Bng. migṇɔ n.m. ‘(quick) blinking (with eyes)’ (with -ṇɔ2 suffix), e.g. seu migṇɔ kɔrɛ ‘he blinks’ (lit.‘he does blinking’), and miṅg-miṅg gaṛṇɔ ‘to blink (with the eyes)’ (with gaṛṇɔ ‘to pull out’) — Klm. ečämik HL n.f. ‘wink or blink of the eye’ (← ec̣ H(L) ‘eyes’) cf. PIE *meigʰ- (perhaps also *meik-) ‘close the eyes’. Sub OIA *micc- ‘close the eyes, blink’ (10118) there are also modern reflexes with -kk- extensions like H. mickānā ‘to wink’; according to Turner, “[a] non-Aryan or widespread onom. word, scarcely. . . to be assigned to a common IE. root. . . ” See also EWA sub MEṢ ‘to open the eyes’ (CDIAL MIṢ *‘blink, open the eyes’) regarding the complexity of this lemma and note also Dravidian Kurkh. miṅkh- ‘to close the eyes’ (Pfeiffer [1972: 28]). Directly related to 10118 are Bng. miċṇɔ ‘to blink; to close one’s eyes’ and mɔċrɔ2 ‘blinking (with eyes)’ (not to be confused with almost identically pronounced mɔċrɔ1 ‘drunk’ which is < OIA matsará- ‘exhilarating’ [9756] [Pa., Pk.] without known modern parallels). Since it is quite impossible that Bng. migṇɔ or miṅg-miṅg gaṛṇɔ is a -kk- extension of miċṇɔ, we have here yet another case of semantic-morphological amalgamations with the Bng. and Klm. forms closest to PIE. Regarding Bng. miṅg- miṅg gaṛṇɔ cf. e.g. Lith. mingù ‘to fall asleep’ (or rather miñga ‘falls asleep’) and see Derksen’s discussion of Proto-Baltic *migla ‘mist, haze’ and *migti ‘fall asleep’ (2015: 317).

text: 1. The Bangāṇī God of Thunder is called guṛku (also meaning ‘thunder’) which is < OIA *guḍ- ‘rumble’ (4180) with a modern parallel in S. to which have to be added Thar. gurgurāi ‘thunder’, Kann. gŭrgŭr ‘thunder’, K. gur-gur ‘a rumble, thunder’ and gagrāy, gɨgrāray ‘thunder’ (Sachdeva et al. [2010: 56]), Klm. āga-guṛant HL-LH ‘it is thundering’ (lit. ‘the sky is thundering’), Garh. gagṛāṭ and giṛaktāḷ ‘thunder’, Ko.S. guḍguḍu ‘thunderbolt’, Ko.kaṇ. guḍguḍ ‘thunder’, and M. gaḍagaḍaṇeṃ ‘to thunder’ — Sant. guɖ guɖ ‘droning, rolling, rumbling (sound of thunder, railway, drums, a running flock of animals, of a water cataract)’, Gtaˈ guɽuŋ-geɽeeke ‘thunder’ — Ora. guṛguṛnā ‘thunder’. Notes: (a) Ju. goɭgoɭi ‘thunder’ reflects OIA (Bālar.) gulugulita- ‘the roaring (of an ele- phant)’, OIA gulagulā- ‘thunder’, gulagulāyate ‘thunders’ (Pa., Pk., but not men- tioned in CDIAL) with Dravidian reflexes found sub DEDR 1837 Ma. guḷūguḷū ‘sound of fruits falling into water’. It appears obvious that the OIA words are borrowings from Munda. Thus, Munda Ju., Dravidian Ma. (and its Dravidian parallels) were borrowed from Munda via an Indo-Aryan language. (b) Note also PN *gur- ‘to rumble, roar, growl, gurgle’ (CINCL 393), PIE *gʰur- ‘to rumble’, according to Bomhard reflected in OIA ghuraghurāyate ‘to utter gur- gling sounds’ (recte ghurghurā- ‘continual growling; Geknurre’ which Mayrhofer characterizes as onomatopoeia which no-one can doubt), cf. also Bomhard’s quotes (ibid.) of Pk. ghurukhaï ‘to thunder’ and S. guguravanā ‘to thunder’. (c) Note also Kartvelian *gurgw- in Georgian grgv-in-v-a ‘to thunder’, Mingre- lian gurg- in gurg-in-i ‘to thunder’, Laz girg-, gurg- in girg-in-i ‘to thunder’ and Svan gurgw- in li-gurgw-n-i ‘to thunder’.
